title: Expectation, variance, and the second moment
dek: Expectation is a linear functional of the sampling law. Variance is the expected squared error around that mean. Neither is a spreadsheet cell until you say which random variable you meant.
story: If Y is a random variable with sampling law f, the expectation E[Y] is the centre of mass of that law: ∑ y f(y) in the discrete case, ∫ y f(y) dy in the continuous case. It is a property of the model, not of yesterday’s sample mean. Linearity does not need independence: E[aU + bV] = a E[U] + b E[V] even when U and V share a household.

Variance is the second central moment, Var(Y) = E[(Y − E[Y])²] = E[Y²] − (E[Y])². It is always nonnegative. Scaling is quadratic: Var(cY) = c² Var(Y). That is why a log transform and a unit change are not cosmetic — they rewrite the variance you will later invert into a standard error.

Covariance Cov(U,V) = E[(U − E[U])(V − E[V])] is the extra term when you add: Var(U+V) = Var(U) + Var(V) + 2 Cov(U,V). Independent implies uncorrelated (covariance zero) for finite-variance variables; the converse is false. A genomics talk that says “uncorrelated, hence independent” has skipped a lemma that is not optional for Gaussians-without-saying-so.
deep: E[g(Y)] is not g(E[Y]) unless g is linear (or you are very lucky). Jensen’s inequality is the adult reminder: for convex φ, φ(E[Y]) ≤ E[φ(Y)]. Geometric-mean CFU and log-MIC analyses live here.

The sample mean Ȳ_n is a different random variable from Y. E[Ȳ_n] = E[Y] under iid sampling (unbiasedness of the mean). Var(Ȳ_n) = Var(Y)/n under iid. That 1/n is the whole point of replication; clustering replaces n with an effective sample size.
Standard deviation sd(Y) = √Var(Y) is on the scale of Y. A standard error is an estimated sd of an estimator, not of Y. Confusing those two is the next plate.
Indicator variables are the bridge to probability: if I_A = 1{A occurs}, then E[I_A] = P(A) and Var(I_A) = P(A)(1 − P(A)). Bernoulli means are probabilities. That is not a pun.
Existence: Cauchy laws have no mean; some heavy-tailed read-count models have infinite variance. Software that always prints a mean is assuming a moment you did not check.

formulas.label: Variance as a second moment
formulas.note: Equivalent to E[(Y − μ)²] with μ = E[Y]. Always ≥ 0 when it exists.

formulas.label: Variance of a sum
formulas.note: Independence zeros the covariance. Clustering does not.

visual.caption: The mean is a one-parameter summary of the law of Y. Variance adds a second moment around that mean. Estimators (Ȳ, s²) are different random variables sitting on top of the same law — they are not extra axioms.
visual.reference: moments live on the law, not on one cell

example.title: Two household smear indicators
example.setup: Y₁, Y₂ are Bernoulli smear-positive indicators, each with E[Yⱼ] = 0.2 and Corr(Y₁,Y₂) = 0.4 (shared exposure). You want E[Y₁+Y₂] and Var(Y₁+Y₂).

steps.title: Linearity first
steps.body: E[Y₁+Y₂] = 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4. Correlation does not enter. The expected number of smear-positive people in the household is 0.4 whether or not they share air.

steps.title: What a naive iid SE would do
steps.body: An iid binomial n = 2 calculation uses Var = 0.32. The clustered variance is 40% larger. Treating households as two independent Bernoulli trials understates uncertainty about the mean.

example.takeaway: Means add regardless. Variances add only after you have named the covariance.

check.prompt: Linearity of expectation E[U+V] = E[U]+E[V] requires:
check.why: Linearity never asked for independence. That demand belongs to the variance-of-a-sum formula without a covariance term.

whyWrong.Independence of U and V: Needed to drop Cov, not to add means.
whyWrong.Gaussian U and V: Linearity is not a Normal lemma.
whyWrong.Var(U+V) = Var(U)+Var(V): That is the uncorrelated case, a different claim.

check.why: Var(cY + d) = c² Var(Y) = 9×4 = 36. Adding 7 does not change variance.

whyWrong.12: That is 3×4, as if variance scaled linearly.
whyWrong.43: That illegally added the constant 7 into a variance.

check.prompt: On the nested-moment plate, why is μ drawn as a reduced model inside a second-moment box?
choices: Because the mean does not exist until you specify a variance
Because a mean is a one-number summary; variance is an extra parameter of the same law, not a different experiment
check.answer: Because a mean is a one-number summary; variance is an extra parameter of the same law, not a different experiment
check.why: Moments are nested summaries of one sampling law. Estimators of those moments are further random variables.

whyWrong.Because the mean does not exist until yo: Means can exist without finite variance (and vice versa, in pathological cases).
whyWrong.Because MSE forbids a mean: MSE is bias² + variance, which uses both.
whyWrong.Because covariance replaces the mean: Covariance is a cross second moment.
